title: From symptom to stage
summary: The clinical pathway: imaging, biopsy and histology, grade and TNM stage, molecular profiling and actionability tiers, liquid biopsy, and how response is measured with RECIST.

shots.title:
From symptom
to stage.
shots.subtitle: What clinicians measure — so you model what matters.
shots.narration: Before you model a clinical problem, you need to know how a patient actually moves from a symptom to a treatment plan, and which measurements exist at each step.

The usual path: a symptom or a screening test, imaging to find the lesion, a biopsy so a pathologist can say what it is, molecular profiling, a stage and grade, and a plan agreed by a multidisciplinary team.

shots.text: **Histology** says what the tumour is. **Grade** says how abnormal its cells look.
shots.narration: The pathologist's microscope remains the reference diagnosis. Separately, the grade describes how abnormal and undifferentiated the cells look, and staging uses it for some cancers.

shots.heading: TNM staging
items: **T** — size and extent of the primary tumour
Combined into stage groups **I to IV**
shots.narration: Solid tumours are staged by TNM: the primary tumour's size and extent, spread to nearby lymph nodes, and distant metastasis — combined into stage groups from one to four. Stage four means it has spread.

shots.text: Profiling finds **actionable** alterations — KRAS G12C, mismatch-repair deficiency — that select a drug.
shots.narration: Molecular profiling looks for alterations that select a therapy. KRAS G12C points to a G12C inhibitor; mismatch-repair deficiency qualifies a patient for checkpoint immunotherapy, whatever the organ.

shots.text: Not every alteration is equal: ESMO's **ESCAT** ranks evidence from **tier I** (routine use) to **tier X** (no evidence).
shots.narration: Not every mutation matters clinically. Europe's ESCAT scale ranks the evidence that targeting an alteration helps, from tier one, ready for routine use, to tier ten, no evidence at all.

shots.text: **Liquid biopsy**: tumour DNA in the blood, sequenced from a blood draw — for profiling and monitoring.
shots.narration: Tumours shed DNA into the blood. Sequencing it — a liquid biopsy — can profile and monitor a cancer from a blood sample, though the biology of this cell-free DNA is still being worked out.

shots.heading: RECIST 1.1 — is it working?
items: Follow at most **5** target lesions (2 per organ)
**Progression**: up **≥20%** and **≥5 mm**, or new lesions
shots.narration: Response is measured with RECIST. Follow up to five target lesions. A partial response is a drop of at least thirty percent in their summed diameters; progression is a rise of at least twenty percent and at least five millimetres.

notes: PR = partial response; PD = progressive disease
percentages from baseline (response) or the smallest sum (progression)
shots.narration: Two worked cases. A summed diameter falling from a hundred to seventy millimetres is a partial response. Rising from twenty to twenty-four is twenty percent — but only four millimetres, so it is not progression.

shots.text: For your research: choose an **endpoint clinicians already measure**. A model of something nobody records is hard to validate.
shots.narration: For your research, the lesson is simple: predict or optimise something clinicians already measure. A model of a quantity nobody records is very hard to validate, and harder to publish.

steps.title: Which tool answers which question?
steps.brief: Clinicians use different tests for different questions. Match each test to the question it answers.

MSI-high solid tumours can receive pembrolizumab, whatever the organ.

cards.text: Summed lesion diameters compared with baseline
Repeated blood tests for circulating tumour DNA
cards.why: Liquid biopsy can monitor disease over time.

questions.prompt: Baseline summed diameter 80 mm; now 52 mm. What is the percentage change? (negative for shrinkage)
questions.explain: (52 − 80)/80 = −35%: at least a 30% decrease, so a partial response.

questions.prompt: Smallest sum so far 20 mm; now 24 mm, no new lesions. Under RECIST 1.1 this is…
options: Not progression: the absolute increase is under 5 mm
questions.explain: Progression needs both ≥20% and ≥5 mm; this is +20% but only 4 mm.
M describes distant metastasis; M1 usually puts the cancer in stage IV.

questions.prompt: An ESCAT tier I alteration is…
questions.explain: Tier I is the strongest evidence; tier X means no evidence of actionability.

steps.title: Homework 5 · A patient's data trail
steps.brief: About 40 minutes. Use a fictional patient — never a real one.

fields.label: 1. Write a short, fictional journey for a patient with KRAS G12C lung cancer: each test, what it showed, and the decision it drove.
2. List the data your journey generated (images, slides, sequences, measurements, outcomes). Which could a researcher realistically obtain, and under what controls?
3. Propose one computational prediction that would change a decision on this journey. Which endpoint would you validate it against?
